title: Multi-Robot Cell Design
contentStatus: Draft for DiFacto review. Title and content to be confirmed.

sections.title: From Operating a Fleet to Designing a Cell
learningObjectives: Recall multi-robot fleet concepts from L2-M4
Understand the Systems Engineer's role in designing, rather than just operating, multi-robot cells
sections.content: L2-M4 taught fleet coordination from an operator's perspective. You learned that collision avoidance, task assignment, and deadlock resolution happen automatically. This module addresses the design side instead: how a Systems Engineer architects a cell containing multiple MoRo units working alongside fixed equipment. The goal is making sure that automatic coordination actually has what it needs to work well.

sections.title: Determining Fleet Size
learningObjectives: Understand general factors influencing how many units a cell requires
Recognize the trade-offs involved in fleet sizing decisions
sections.content: Fleet size for a cell depends on three things. Throughput requirements - how much material needs to move, and how quickly. Physical space - more units need more room to operate without excessive congestion. And redundancy needs - whether the cell can tolerate a unit being temporarily out of service. Oversizing wastes capital. Undersizing creates a throughput bottleneck. Getting this right requires modeling actual operational demand, not guessing.

keyTerms.note: How much material a cell moves in a given period.
Spare capacity, such as an extra unit, so the cell keeps working when one part is unavailable.

sections.title: Spatial Design for Multi-Unit Operation
learningObjectives: Understand spatial design considerations specific to multiple coordinated units
Recognize how this connects to zone management (shared paths and reserved routes)
sections.content: Spatial design for a multi-robot cell builds directly on zone management - the shared paths and reserved routes that Programmers configure in L3B-M3. That means identifying where shared paths and reserved routes make sense given the physical layout. It also means ensuring adequate clearance for multiple units operating simultaneously, without creating chronic congestion points.

sections.title: Coordinating Multiple Units with Fixed Equipment
learningObjectives: Understand the added complexity when multiple units interact with the same fixed equipment
sections.content: When multiple MoRo units need to interact with the same fixed machine - the same CNC station, for example - the cell design needs to handle queuing. Units need to wait their turn appropriately rather than conflicting. This builds on the request-ready-complete handshake used with fixed machines (taught to Programmers in L3B-M4), now applied where multiple units compete for the same resource.

keyTerms.note: Automated machine tools controlled by programmed instructions, commonly loaded and unloaded by MoRo in machine tending applications.
The agreed exchange of signals (request, ready, complete) that lets MoRo and a fixed machine hand work to each other safely.

sections.title: Designing for Graceful Degradation
learningObjectives: Understand the principle of graceful degradation in multi-robot cell design
Recognize why this matters for operational resilience
sections.content: A well-designed multi-robot cell continues operating at reduced capacity if one unit goes offline for maintenance or a fault. The entire cell's throughput shouldn't collapse just because one unit is down. Designing for this means avoiding single points of failure, where the whole cell's function depends on every unit being simultaneously available.

keyTerms.note: One component whose failure stops the whole cell.
Continuing to operate at reduced capacity when part of the system fails, instead of stopping completely.

sections.title: Validating a Multi-Robot Cell Design
learningObjectives: Understand how to validate a cell design before full deployment
Recognize the value of phased rollout for multi-unit deployments
sections.content: Validating a multi-robot cell design benefits from a phased approach. Start with fewer units than the final target. Confirm coordination behaves as expected. Then scale up incrementally, rather than deploying the full fleet size at once. This mirrors the broader principle of validating incrementally, consistent with testing practices covered throughout this curriculum.

questions.question: What does this module address, building on L2-M4's fleet concepts?
options: A deeper look at operating one MoRo unit from the dashboard during a normal shift, with its alerts
The design side: how an engineer architects a cell with several units and fixed equipment
Instructions for repairing a unit that has left the fleet
questions.feedback: Correct. This module covers the design side of multi-robot cells, building on L2-M4's operational foundation.

questions.question: What factors influence fleet sizing for a cell?
options: Only the cost of each unit and the budget set for the project
The total payload weight of the heaviest part the cell will ever handle
Throughput, floor space, and redundancy needs
questions.feedback: Correct. Fleet sizing balances throughput demand, space, and redundancy considerations.

questions.question: When several units use the same CNC station, what does the cell design need to handle?
options: Queuing, so units wait their turn instead of conflicting
Charging, so every unit docks at the same moment to keep timing equal
Mapping, so each unit rebuilds the floor map before every visit
questions.feedback: Correct. When units compete for the same machine, the design must make them queue rather than conflict.

questions.question: What does 'graceful degradation' mean in cell design?
options: Each unit slowly loses speed as its wheels and battery age
The cell shuts down in a controlled order when any unit fails
The cell keeps working at reduced capacity when one unit is unavailable
questions.feedback: Correct. Graceful degradation avoids single points of failure that would collapse the whole cell's function.

questions.question: What's a recommended approach to validating a new multi-robot cell design?
options: Start with fewer units, confirm coordination works, then scale up in steps
Deploy the full fleet at once, so that any coordination problems show up as early as possible
Test one unit alone and assume the others will behave the same way
questions.feedback: Correct. Phased, incremental validation reduces risk compared to full deployment at once.
